article.headline: The Chart That Explains the AI Trade: OpenAI's Supply Chain Has Lapped Google's
article.lede: A Bloomberg custom index tracking the stocks most exposed to OpenAI's build-out has roughly tripled since late 2024, while a parallel basket of Google-ecosystem suppliers has gone nowhere. Posted without comment by a fintech account ahead of what turned out to be a $110–122 billion fundraise, the chart is a blunt verdict on which AI platform the market believes is winning the infrastructure cycle.
article.body:
The two indices in the Bloomberg chart are not products the terminal sells by name; they are analyst-constructed baskets — a common practice for tracking thematic exposure when no listed ETF exists. The Google Ecosystem basket groups Alphabet (GOOG) with four contract manufacturers and component suppliers that depend heavily on its data-centre capital spending: Broadcom (AVGO), which designs Google’s custom tensor processing unit (TPU) silicon; Celestica (CLS), which assembles TPU server racks; Lumentum (LITE), which supplies the optical transceivers and switches that carry traffic inside Google’s clusters; and TTM Technologies (TTMI), a printed-circuit-board (PCB) fabricator with a 20–30 percent share of Google’s TPU PCB orders. The OpenAI basket is broader and more financially leveraged: NVIDIA (NVDA), the GPU monopolist that supplies nearly every training cluster on the planet; SoftBank (SFTBY), OpenAI’s lead financial backer and co-chair of the Stargate joint venture; Oracle (ORCL), which is committing data-centre capacity to Stargate; AMD, the secondary GPU alternative; Microsoft (MSFT), OpenAI’s cloud host on Azure; and CoreWeave (CRWV), the neocloud — a GPU-specialist cloud provider that rents compute to AI companies rather than building general-purpose infrastructure — that went public in March 2025 and holds over $66 billion in contracted backlog from Microsoft, OpenAI, and Meta.

The chart was posted on or around 2 February 2026, roughly three weeks before OpenAI closed a $110 billion funding round at a $730 billion valuation, later upsized to $122 billion at $852 billion by end of March. The phrase mega raise in the tweet referred to that round, which was already being discussed in deal circles. Amazon anchored with $50 billion, NVIDIA put in $30 billion, and SoftBank contributed another $30 billion — each of which is itself a constituent of the OpenAI basket, meaning the index was, in part, tracking companies writing cheques into the very entity that would validate their investment thesis.

The performance gap is striking but not mysterious. Google’s capex ecosystem is a set of contract relationships: Celestica assembles servers, TTM makes boards, Lumentum ships optics. Each link in that chain earns thin manufacturing margins, and its revenue is capped by Google’s own spending decisions — which, during 2025, shifted some TPU assembly to Taiwanese OEMs including Inventec, clipping Celestica directly. Google itself is a strong AI competitor (its Gemini models, TPU silicon, and DeepMind research are world-class), but the Google basket is not Google; it is a set of subcontractors whose fortunes depend on one customer’s procurement choices. The OpenAI basket, by contrast, captures the demand aggregator (OpenAI itself, via NVIDIA and ORCL revenues), the infrastructure financier (SoftBank), and the pure-play neocloud (CoreWeave) — companies whose equity valuations are directly leveraged to AI capacity expansion in a way that PCB manufacturers and server assemblers simply are not.

The Stargate joint venture (a $500 billion planned AI data-centre programme co-owned by OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle, and Abu Dhabi’s MGX) is the single largest articulation of that leverage. When Stargate buys GPU servers, NVIDIA ships chips, Oracle provides land and power, CoreWeave leases adjacent GPU capacity, and SoftBank’s equity in the venture appreciates. The Google basket has no equivalent flywheel. Lumentum does sell optics into NVIDIA’s reference designs and announced a $2 billion investment from NVIDIA in early 2026, but that is a recent pivot, not the thesis that defined the Google basket over the period the chart covers.

A note of caution belongs here. The OpenAI basket’s outperformance through February 2026 was followed by turbulence: in late April, reports emerged that OpenAI had missed its own targets for new user acquisition and sales, triggering a sharp sell-off in NVDA, ORCL, and CRWV in a single session. The Bloomberg opinion desk ran a piece arguing that an OpenAI-specific bubble need not imply an AI infrastructure bubble more broadly — a distinction the market did not immediately make. The chart @DratchCap posted was a snapshot of euphoria at near-peak, not a forward projection. What it genuinely captures is the structural question the AI cycle keeps posing: does value accrue to the platform that aggregates demand, or to the manufacturers that fulfil it? So far, the market’s answer has been unambiguous.

concepts.definition: A basket of companies whose revenues are primarily driven by the capital-expenditure decisions of a single large technology platform. When that platform accelerates data-centre spending, the ecosystem suppliers benefit; when it slows or diversifies procurement, they are exposed. The term is used here to describe the Bloomberg-constructed indices grouping Google’s and OpenAI’s respective hardware supply chains.

A cloud provider that specialises exclusively in GPU compute, renting accelerator capacity to AI developers and model companies rather than offering the broad suite of storage, networking, and application services that hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) provide. CoreWeave is the canonical example; it went public in March 2025 and holds multi-year capacity contracts with Microsoft, OpenAI, and Meta.

A joint venture announced in January 2025 by OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle, and Abu Dhabi’s MGX with a stated plan to invest up to $500 billion in AI data-centre infrastructure in the United States by 2029. SoftBank and OpenAI are the lead financial and operational partners respectively. Oracle provides data-centre capacity and is an equity participant. The project is the largest single articulation of the OpenAI supply-chain investment thesis.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

sources.title: Nvidia Stock Analysis 2026: AI Demand — Intellectia
NVIDIA Stock Forecast: AI Chip Demand — TIKR

ticker_orcl.name: Oracle Corporation
ticker_orcl.blurb: Oracle is an enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company founded by Larry Ellison in 1977 and headquartered in Austin, Texas. Its core businesses are database software (Oracle Database remains the dominant enterprise RDBMS by revenue), cloud applications (ERP, HCM, and CX via Oracle Fusion and NetSuite), and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), its IaaS platform. OCI entered the AI infrastructure race later than AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud but has emerged as a preferred hyperscale partner for OpenAI and other large AI workloads, partly due to competitive GPU pricing and multi-region data-centre commitments. Oracle is an equity participant in the Stargate joint venture alongside OpenAI and SoftBank.
ticker_orcl.recent: Oracle's fiscal Q3 2026 (ending February 2026) was described by management as the strongest quarter in more than 15 years: total revenue rose 22% year-on-year to $17.2 billion, cloud revenue jumped 44% to $8.9 billion, and GPU-related cloud revenue grew 177% year-on-year in the prior quarter. The company reported a $523 billion remaining performance-obligation backlog — driven by AI mega-deals with OpenAI and Meta — and committed approximately $50 billion in capital expenditure for fiscal 2026. BNP Paribas analysts estimated that Oracle's 4.5 gigawatt Stargate capacity commitment could eventually generate $30–60 billion in annual revenue.

ticker_crwv.name: CoreWeave, Inc.
ticker_crwv.blurb: CoreWeave is a neocloud — a GPU-specialist cloud provider that rents NVIDIA accelerator capacity to AI developers, research labs, and enterprises rather than offering the broad service catalogue of a hyperscaler. Founded in 2017 as a cryptocurrency mining operation and pivoted to GPU cloud in 2019, it operates more than 40 data centres with roughly 250,000 NVIDIA GPUs. Its commercial model is long-term capacity contracts — often three to seven years — which produce a large, predictable backlog but require heavy upfront debt-financed capital expenditure. CoreWeave went public on NASDAQ on 28 March 2025 at $40 per share, valuing the company at approximately $23 billion fully diluted. NVIDIA invested $2 billion in CoreWeave at $87.20 per share in January 2026, cementing the symbiotic relationship between the two companies.
ticker_crwv.recent: CoreWeave reported $5.1 billion in revenue for full-year 2025, up 170% year-on-year, with quarterly revenue reaching $1.57 billion in Q4. Microsoft accounted for approximately 67% of FY2025 revenue. OpenAI has contracted up to $22.4 billion in cumulative commitments, and Meta signed a $14.2 billion agreement through December 2031. Total remaining performance obligations represent roughly 13 years of revenue at current run rates. In April 2026, CoreWeave priced an upsized $3.5 billion convertible senior notes offering and announced a multi-year GPU capacity agreement with Anthropic.

ticker_goog.name: Alphabet Inc. (Class C)
ticker_goog.blurb: Alphabet is the parent company of Google, headquartered in Mountain View, California. Its principal revenue source is Google Search advertising, which has historically contributed approximately 55–60% of total revenue, supplemented by YouTube advertising, Google Cloud, and hardware. Google Cloud (GCP) is Alphabet's fastest-growing segment and competes directly with AWS and Azure for enterprise and AI workloads. Alphabet designs its own AI accelerators — tensor processing units (TPUs) — through Google DeepMind, reducing reliance on NVIDIA GPUs and enabling tight hardware-software co-design. GOOG is the Class C non-voting share; GOOGL is the Class A voting share. Both trade on NASDAQ.
ticker_goog.recent: Alphabet reported Google Cloud revenue growing 48% year-on-year in Q4 2025, with a $240 billion backlog — a 55% sequential jump. Gemini, Google's flagship AI model family, reached 750 million monthly active users with serving costs per unit down 78% over 2025 through model and hardware optimisations. Alphabet outlined 2026 capital expenditures of $175–185 billion, more than double its 2025 spend, to support AI infrastructure expansion. Google Cloud Next 2026 showcased 8th-generation TPUs (split into TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference) and Gemini Enterprise, positioning Alphabet as a serious competitor to the OpenAI ecosystem for enterprise agentic AI workloads.

ticker_avgo.name: Broadcom Inc.
ticker_avgo.blurb: Broadcom is a diversified semiconductor and infrastructure software company formed through a series of acquisitions, most recently VMware (closed 2023). Its chip portfolio spans networking ASICs (custom chips for hyperscaler AI clusters), enterprise storage controllers, WiFi silicon, and set-top-box processors. Broadcom's AI networking chips — particularly its Tomahawk Ethernet switching ASICs and custom AI accelerators built for Google, Meta, and Apple — have made it a second-tier AI infrastructure beneficiary behind NVIDIA. The VMware acquisition added high-margin enterprise software revenue that meaningfully improved the company's margin profile.
ticker_avgo.recent: Broadcom's FY2026 revenue (ending Oct 2026) is on track to exceed $65 billion, with AI-related chip revenue growing rapidly as hyperscalers expand custom silicon programs. Forward EPS growth of 56.3% and a forward P/E of ~23.4x produce a PEG of 0.42 — among the best risk-adjusted valuations in large-cap technology. CEO Hock Tan has guided to $60–90 billion in AI chip revenue by 2027 from three major hyperscaler customers alone.

sources.title: NVIDIA vs TSMC vs Broadcom: AI Chip Stocks 2026 — HeyGoTrade

ticker_cls.description: Celestica is a Canadian EMS (Electronics Manufacturing Services) company that has rapidly become one of the leading contract manufacturers for AI infrastructure — assembling AI servers, networking switches, storage arrays, and hardware platform solutions for hyperscale data center operators. Its Connectivity and Cloud segment grew 76% year-over-year in Q1 2026. Q1 2026 revenue of $4.05 billion (+53% YoY) drove management to raise full-year 2026 guidance to $17 billion with $8.75 adjusted EPS. The company is expanding capacity in Thailand and building a major new Texas facility.
ticker_cls.blurb: Celestica is a Canadian EMS (Electronics Manufacturing Services) company that has rapidly become one of the leading contract manufacturers for AI infrastructure — assembling AI servers, networking switches, storage arrays, and hardware platform solutions for hyperscale data center operators. The company is expanding capacity in Thailand and building a major new Texas facility.
ticker_cls.recent: Q1 2026 revenue of $4.05 billion (+53% YoY) drove management to raise full-year 2026 guidance to $17 billion with $8.75 adjusted EPS. The Connectivity and Cloud segment grew 76% year-over-year in the quarter.

ticker_lite.name: Lumentum Holdings Inc.
ticker_lite.blurb: Lumentum makes the lasers, optical chips, and components that go into the high-speed transceivers wiring AI data centres together. Spun out of JDSU in 2015, it spent its first decade as a 3D-sensing and telecom-optics supplier of moderate growth. The AI-cluster build-out has remade it into one of the principal upstream beneficiaries of hyperscaler capex, alongside Coherent Corp.
ticker_lite.recent: Q1 fiscal-2026 set record revenue, with management citing AI-driven demand and an order book that runs into 2027. In March 2026 Nvidia announced a roughly $2 billion strategic investment paired with multi-year purchase commitments for co-packaged-optics components. The company joined the S&P 500 in March 2026; shares have surged on AI demand, leaving the stock at a forward P/E in the 60s, materially above peers.

ticker_ttmi.name: TTM Technologies, Inc.
ticker_ttmi.blurb: TTM Technologies is the largest printed-circuit-board (PCB) manufacturer in North America and one of the top five globally, headquartered in Santa Ana, California. PCBs are the laminated boards that mechanically support and electrically connect electronic components in virtually every device — from fighter jets to AI server racks. TTM's end markets include aerospace and defence (roughly 45% of revenue), data-centre computing (growing rapidly from a 14% base), medical and industrial, automotive, and networking. The company also produces radio-frequency and specialty (RF&S) components. TTM has historically supplied PCBs for Google's tensor processing unit (TPU) server programmes alongside Korea's ISU, maintaining an estimated 20–30% market share in that segment.
ticker_ttmi.recent: TTM's data-centre computing segment grew approximately 57% in 2025, driven by ultra-HDI (high-density interconnect) board demand for AI server programmes. In July 2025, the company acquired a 750,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, and secured land rights in Penang, Malaysia, to support high-volume US production of advanced PCBs for AI and defence. The company is positioned as a beneficiary of US government reshoring requirements for defence electronics and growing domestic AI infrastructure investment.

ticker_sftby.name: SoftBank Group Corp. (ADR)
ticker_sftby.blurb: SFTBY is the American Depositary Receipt (ADR) for SoftBank Group Corp., the Japanese technology conglomerate founded by Masayoshi Son. SoftBank is best known as a technology investment vehicle — through its Vision Fund I ($100 billion, 2017) and Vision Fund II, it took stakes in Uber, WeWork, DoorDash, ARM Holdings, and hundreds of other companies. ARM Holdings (NASDAQ: ARM), which SoftBank retained after a partial IPO in 2023, remains its single largest asset. SoftBank has repositioned itself since 2024 as the lead financial architect of AI infrastructure, with Masayoshi Son publicly framing artificial superintelligence as a civilisational imperative. Each ADR represents one-half of one ordinary SoftBank share.
ticker_sftby.recent: SoftBank completed a $41 billion investment in OpenAI — the largest single external investment in an AI company on record — giving it approximately 11% of the ChatGPT maker. SoftBank is the lead financial partner in the Stargate joint venture, a $500 billion planned US AI data-centre programme co-founded with OpenAI, Oracle, and Abu Dhabi's MGX. SoftBank sold its entire $5.8 billion Nvidia stake and $4.8 billion of its T-Mobile stake to fund these AI commitments. SB Energy (a SoftBank subsidiary) is developing multi-gigawatt data-centre campuses expected to enter service in 2026, with a $3 billion Ohio manufacturing facility also underway.

ticker_amd.name: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
ticker_amd.blurb: AMD is a fabless semiconductor company that designs CPUs (EPYC for data centres, Ryzen for consumer PCs) and GPUs (Instinct for AI/HPC, Radeon for gaming and workstations). Under CEO Lisa Su, AMD has taken significant data-centre CPU market share from Intel with its EPYC server processors, which now command an estimated 30%+ of the x86 server CPU market. AMD's MI300X and MI350 AI accelerators compete directly with NVIDIA's H100/H200 family and are gaining traction with hyperscalers seeking GPU supply alternatives. All AMD chips are manufactured by TSMC.
ticker_amd.recent: AMD reported strong 2025 revenue growth led by EPYC and Instinct, with data-centre revenue crossing $12 billion annually. Forward P/E of ~32.6x on 63.8% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 0.51 — compelling for a company with clear data-centre CPU momentum and an AI accelerator portfolio that is gaining customer adoption. NVIDIA's dominant CUDA ecosystem remains the primary competitive barrier for AMD's GPU ambitions.

ticker_msft.name: Microsoft Corporation
ticker_msft.description: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.

ticker_msft.recent: As of early May 2026, MSFT trades near $413 — down approximately 25.6% from its July 31, 2025 all-time high of $555.45 and -15.7% YTD — after touching a March 28 correction low of $356.07. The drawdown carried the stock briefly below its 200-week moving average for the first time in roughly 13 years (prior touches: 2009, 2018, 2020, 2022). Revenue grew 18% YoY with Azure +40%, while annualized AI revenue reached approximately $37 billion; calendar-2026 capex is projected near $190 billion and free cash flow contracted -22% YoY. Forward P/E is approximately 24.4.
